items.title: Outage Chaos: Who Turned Off All The Computer?
items.author: Starchy Grant
items.content: It's been a tough couple of weeks for anyone trying to use email, fly, spend money, use an Apple device*, or do signals intelligence. Technical service outages are nothing new, but why do so many big ones seem to be happening all at once? Are hackers, AI, and international conflicts to blame? And what can we do about it? Since most service interruptions don't make the news, it's hard to get a baseline on how often we see them happen normally. But after a major incident like the Microsoft cloud outage on November 12, any smaller disruption is more likely to become a story as part of a pattern instead of an isolated incident. We would have heard plenty about the Air Traffic Control problems anyway, but the November 18 disruption to the PlayStation Network might have gotten less attention. There might appear to be a spike or an upward trend in outages, but we can't easily verify that, and the increased coverage will tend to make it seem more significant and interconnected than it necessarily is regardless. One boring reason we might see an uptick in problems right now is the date on the calendar. With Thanksgiving travel, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, Giving Tuesday, and Surveillance Sunday (we assume) all coming up, organizations often schedule major system updates for the first three weeks of November. This helps them prepare for holiday traffic, and lets them shift the outage risk to the time before those dates when they may consider it far more important to maintain reliable service. While none of these particular outages have yet been directly attributed to AI (or to malicious hackers), bank CEOs and the NSA briefed congress and reportedly attributed at least some of them to rushed attempts to patch vulnerabilities found by AI. That’s understandable: all software updates carry risk, and companies and governments are having to deploy more updates, and faster, than they’ve ever needed to before. Some of those updates are to important infrastructure, where an outage would be very disruptive, but the impact of leaving vulnerabilities unpatched would be even worse. Vulnerabilities are a type of software bug that affects security. Once a vulnerability is found in a given piece of software and disclosed, typically the software maker will release a patch fixing that vulnerability. That’s why so many update notes say things like “performance improvements and security fixes” — the security fixes are patches to vulnerabilities. Companies and governments that run infrastructure face a challenging tradeoff: deploy patches quickly or slowly and cautiously? Patching quickly is important to keep systems secure. But every software update runs a risk: any change to a deployed system can have unintended consequences that snowball into a disastrous outage. This exacerbates a much deeper problem long discussed in the engineering culture of many, if not most organizations. Keeping networks, servers, and applications not just secure but resilient in the face of patches, reboots, and capacity changes requires an investment in staff, time, hardware, and processes for frequent maintenance, redundant systems, realistic staging environments, automated rollbacks, monitoring, and pre-deployment testing. These investments are rarely as attractive to decision-makers as a new product or feature, or at times, sadly, as layoffs. This should come as no surprise when we think of our apps, web sites, airlines, and bank cards as supported by electronic infrastructure. As in the more visible physical world, maintenance can only be deferred for so long before the costs become immediate and dramatic. We accept the cost of an occasional short term bridge closure to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse, and highway departments schedule road work nearly every night of the year to repair and prevent the worst potholes. When this kind of work is endlessly deferred in the world of software, we speak of technical debt: issues we already know about that aren't causing a big enough problem right now to divert us from other work, but that, if left unaddressed, can easily multiply and interact to cause outages or other complications. This can show up as routine steps that have to be done by hand instead of automatically on a schedule, a programmer's shortcut that works well in one specific situation but is more fragile in general, an operating system six months (or years) overdue for a reboot, or a piece of networking hardware no longer supported for patches by its manufacturer. On the other hand, when maintenance work is well-resourced and routine, it should be rare for even major security updates to cause significant issues. What’s needed in the short term is a big investment in the people and training needed to roll out patches promptly and safely. What’s needed in the long term is a big investment in software security, eliminating entire classes of vulnerabilities, like memory safety, before they are ever written. For organizations that have gotten used to patching slowly and cautiously, suddenly switching gears to patching quickly is a big challenge. And the flood of vulnerability disclosures enabled by AI means that everyone is being asked to switch gears like that at once. Fortunately, it’s not a zero-sum game: patches can be rolled out quickly and cautiously, with investments in reducing technical debt and expanding maintenance budgets as described above. These measures are expensive and time-consuming, but necessary. For governments asking how to respond to AI-enabled cybersecurity threats, investing in the people and training necessary to stay on top of patches will pay big dividends in reliability and security. For individuals, consider the trade-offs when relying on a single provider for many services you rely on. Consumer cloud and device offerings tie together many of the things we need to function on a daily basis like email, messaging, file storage, and even payments, but that convenience and simplicity comes with the risk of losing access to it all if that service goes offline (or suspends your account). Trying out interoperable alternatives is a great way to reduce your reliance on a single company. Finally, for any critical data, learn the 3-2-1 rule for backups: Keep three different copies on two different types of storage with one copy in a different physical location. For many users, a laptop or other personal device, cloud storage, and a local backup disk exemplify this rule, as long as the laptop stores data on its own drives, not only in the cloud. Among other things, the accelerated rollout of AI has made it all the more critical to reinvest in people and systems to keep our software, networks, governments, and interconnected world stable. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

items.title: Scaling Linear’s GTM to $100M ARR — Cristina Cordova, COO
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.content: Open video on YouTube ↗ Linear was founded to build a better issue tracker. Seven years and $134 million in funding later, its CEO Karri Saarinen published a post titled "Issue tracking is dead." In this episode, we chat with Cristina Cordova, COO of Linear, about how the company navigated that and how its go-to-market changed along the way. Cristina spent seven and a half years at Stripe, led platform and partnerships at Notion, and was a partner at First Round before joining Linear in 2023. Linear's founders built it after living with legacy issue trackers at Coinbase, Airbnb and Uber, and it spread self-serve through startups like Vercel and Ramp. When she joined, Linear had about 40 people and one salesperson. Since then it has shipped an MCP server, a platform for building agents into Linear, integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot, and its own Linear Agent. Agents created 3% of Linear's work a year ago. Now it's more than half. Linear passed $100 million in ARR this year with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention, and in August employees sold $99 million in stock at a $2.5 billion valuation. We talk about why she stopped chasing enterprise deals three weeks after joining, why Linear has never hired a single SDR, why it won't let an LLM answer support tickets on its own, and what the AI budgets behind $100M-in-months ARR mean for everyone else. Half the work on Linear is now created by agents Linear shipped its MCP server in May 2025, and Cristina says it was basically the first in its category. A year and a half later, more than half the issues created in Linear come from agents. That doesn't mean Linear wants to be a database with an MCP server on top. Cristina thinks SaaS companies settling for that are making a big mistake. If the agent workflows inside your product aren't better than the ones outside it, nobody has a reason to open your app. So she watches two lines: agent usage and app usage. If agent usage climbs and app usage doesn't, you're becoming a commodity. At Linear, both are up and to the right, because people still come back to the app to see and coordinate the work. Jump to the MCP discussion → "Issue tracking is dead" When Karri published "Issue tracking is dead" in March, most of Linear's customers agreed with him. Then they asked the obvious question: so what am I buying? Linear's answer is a product development system built around agent orchestration, where humans stop doing the manual work of filing, labeling, assigning and closing issues. Customers had been pushing it there. Most of the frontier AI labs run on Linear and wanted it to move faster. Pre-AI companies like Ramp and Coinbase were building their own internal agents and needed an API to plug them into Linear. Cristina says Linear is lucky it's small enough to cannibalize itself. Google has a much harder problem: put an AI answer above every search result, and fewer people look at the ads. Jump to the "issue tracking is dead" discussion → The AI budget behind $100M in months The thing speeding up purchases right now, Cristina says, is AI budget. Companies carved out money for AI tools that didn't exist before, and any product that fits inside it skips the usual fight for spend. At some companies that budget is very high. It's already starting to change. Buyers are signing one-year deals and paid pilots, not three-year contracts, because nobody knows what they'll want in two years. And some overnight-$100M stories are a handful of $30 to $40 million contracts with defense companies or giant law firms. That's a very different business from Linear's 40,000 paying customers on what was, until June, entirely seat-based pricing. When those one-year deals come up for renewal, we'll find out whose ARR was real. Jump to the AI budget discussion → Linear threw out its 2025 enterprise roadmap Three weeks after joining in 2023, Cristina crossed "move upmarket to enterprise" off Linear's company goals. It had one salesperson. She went after growth-stage companies that would have to rip out an existing tool instead, the same way Stripe won new businesses long before it won switchers. Linear finally declared an enterprise push in 2025, with a roadmap full of features for large organizations. Then agents happened. Linear built an MCP server, an agents platform with a whole new set of APIs, and integrations with Codex, Cursor and GitHub Copilot. None of it was planned, and a lot of the enterprise work never got done. Cristina chose to race ahead anyway. Competitors waited, and enterprises started putting Linear on their shortlists. Jump to the enterprise roadmap discussion → No SDRs, no forward deployed engineers Linear has never hired a single SDR. Cristina thinks the qualification call wastes the customer's time: they want a demo, not questions about their budget. AEs do their own outbound, with tooling to keep it personal. It doesn't do forward deployed engineering either. Linear should be easy enough to adopt that nobody needs access to your systems. Solutions engineers sell alongside enterprise AEs instead, sometimes building a working ServiceNow integration overnight to show a prospect it can be done. Cristina adds that an opinionated tool gives agents cleaner data than one where every team defines "bug" differently. Support stays in-house, and Linear won't let an LLM answer tickets on its own. AI drafts replies and a human decides what goes out. Customers sometimes assume the replies are AI because they arrive so fast. In three and a half years, Cristina has never had an escalation over a bad support experience. Jump to the sales team discussion → Everyone wants outcome-based pricing Cristina would love a model like Intercom's Fin, which charges for each support conversation its AI resolves. It's harder for Linear. What is auto-triaging a bug to the right team worth when one company thinks that's the PM's job and another doesn't? Until someone cracks that, Linear charges for what costs it money and keeps the rest free. Seats stay. Linear Agent chat is free even though it runs on frontier models. In coding sessions, users pick OpenAI or Anthropic models and harnesses, and Linear passes through the published API price plus a small markup. Loops run on AI credits. Linear doesn't start charging for things that used to be free. New AI features launch as free betas with notice that pricing is coming, and prices start high and come down rather than the other way around. Jump to the pricing discussion → Why not hire 100 salespeople? Cristina says Linear runs on about half the headcount of companies at its stage and revenue. A sales team bigger than the rest of the company would have cost it the trust engineering now has in sales. From Stripe she brought a 40% rule: at least 40% of the company should be engineering, product, design and data. If sales wanted more people, it helped recruit engineers first. Linear has no hard rule, but one of the first things she built was a headcount spreadsheet by function, and she still watches the ratio. Hiring is slow on purpose. Candidates do a work trial on a real problem. Hers was writing Linear's go-to-market plan for the next six to twelve months, which then became her job. At about 170 people, the only C-suite is the founders and her. Jump to the hiring discussion → Show notes Linear — the product development system where Cristina is COO. Sharing Linear's growth with the people building it — the August tender at a $2.5 billion valuation, with more than 40,000 paying customers and 177% net revenue retention. Issue tracking is dead — Karri's March post on why Linear is building for agents. Linear MCP server — the May 2025 launch Cristina says was basically a first for the category. Introducing Linear Agent — the built-in agent whose chat Linear keeps free. How we built Triage Intelligence — the feature that suggests labels and catches duplicates in incoming issues, Cristina's example of AI that doesn't need to be an agent Coding sessions in Linear — the June launch that ended Linear's all-seat pricing, running Claude Code and Codex on AI credits. Introducing Loops — recurring agent jobs, also billed with AI credits. Intercom Fin pricing — $0.99 per resolved conversation, the outcome-based model Cristina wishes fit Linear. items.title: nginx2root: Five new nginx vulnerabilities, and how Cloudflare protects origins from the worst of them
items.author: Dan Jones
items.content: On November 18, 2026, F5 and nginx.org disclosed ten vulnerabilities in nginx. Five of them, detailed by the Xint research team and published under the name nginx2root, are memory corruption flaws that an unauthenticated attacker can use to crash an nginx worker or, per Xint's research, run commands on the server. Xint also found a Linux kernel bug that turns that foothold into root on the host, including from inside a Docker container. Other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently: F5 also credits Rapid7, Wiz Research and Ikotas Labs for CVE-2026-123007, and Metnir, Wiz Research, and Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 for CVE-2026-123633. nginx is an HTTP web server that also serves as reverse proxy, content cache, load balancer, TCP/UDP proxy server, and mail proxy server. nginx runs a large share of the world's web servers, so this is a patch-now event. But if your nginx server is reachable only through Cloudflare's proxy, attackers cannot reach the vulnerable code paths for the most serious of these bugs, giving you protection while you update your servers. Here is where Cloudflare stands, what that protection covers, where it stops, and how the bugs work. The short version Cloudflare's edge is not affected. Much of the proxy that handles customer traffic at our edge now runs on FL2, written in Rust. We reviewed the parts still built on our heavily modified nginx fork against all five bugs before disclosure, and an update closing the related code paths finished rolling out globally before the vulnerabilities were published. The same releases fix five other nginx CVEs, including CVE-2026-118899, an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3. Origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are shielded from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. For proxied hostnames, Cloudflare terminates every client HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connection at our edge and opens a separate connection to your origin. The attacker's frames never reach your nginx. The resolver and mail proxy vulnerabilities depend on specific configuration. Many configurations of nginx will not be vulnerable, but the safest way to be sure is to update your install or disable features. You should still patch. Update to nginx 1.30.7 or 1.31.9 (or your vendor's fixed build) and restart. Some configurations, covered below, are not protected by the proxy. What was disclosed nginx2root is five independent bugs. Each one works on its own and each one needs a different configuration. CVE Bug class Affected configuration First affected release CVE-2026-123007 Integer overflow leading to out-of-bounds heap read/write HTTP/2 enabled 1.9.5 (2015) CVE-2026-123633 Use-after-free HTTP/2 with proxy_pass to a backend, worker low on worker_connections 1.19.7 CVE-2026-121810 Use-after-free HTTP/3 (QUIC) with proxy_pass to a backend 1.25.0 CVE-2026-123634 Use-after-free resolver + proxy_pass with variables + a subrequest (mirror or SSI) 0.6.18 CVE-2026-113425 Use-after-free Mail proxy with proxy on and auth_http 0.5.33 F5 rates each one High (CVSS 3.1: 8.1) and Critical (CVSS 4.0: 9.2), and notes that code execution requires disabling or bypassing ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomization). For CVE-2026-123007, Xint's write-up shows how it leaked memory addresses to do exactly that. CVE-2026-123007 is the one to worry about most. It only needs HTTP/2 turned on, which is commonly enabled on TLS deployments, and it has been in every nginx release since HTTP/2 support shipped in 1.9.5. Xint ran the exploit over the public Internet against servers on AWS, GCP and Azure. Xint searched Shodan on November 10, before the disclosure, and found 56.7 million hosts matching product:nginx. Of the 11.94 million that reported a version, 98.9% fell in the affected range. As of November 19, Censys's nginx2root exposure tracker counts about 8.8 million services running a potentially affected version with HTTP/2 enabled. Version strings don't prove a host is vulnerable, since distributions backport fixes, but the exposure is large. The same nginx releases also fix five other bugs. The most serious, CVE-2026-118899, is an infinite loop when reading a request body over TLS 1.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker stall a worker, in nginx 1.13.0 and later. The Linux kernel bug is the sixth part of nginx2root. Xint found a use-after-free in the kernel's SCTP send path, present since Linux 4.15 (2018): while a send operation waits, its SCTP association can be moved to another socket, and the waiting send can then free it. An attacker who already runs code as the nginx worker can use it to gain root on the host, and Xint did this from an nginx running inside a Docker container. Many distributions load the SCTP module automatically the first time a program opens an SCTP socket, so hosts that never use SCTP can still be exposed. As of November 18, no kernel fix was available and Xint was withholding the details until there is one. As of November 19, none of the five nginx2root CVEs is in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, and we have not seen reports of exploitation in the wild. Xint and Wiz Research have not released their exploits. Rapid7 has published a proof of concept, which it describes as suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started local container. Fake 'exploits' are also circulating on GitHub. Why Cloudflare's proxy protects your origin nginx2root's most dangerous bugs live in how nginx parses and manages HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 connections. To trigger them, an attacker has to send a carefully ordered stream of protocol frames directly to the nginx process: billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames, a SETTINGS frame that holds response data back, PING frames that fill the send buffers, partial HEADERS frames, RST_STREAM at exactly the right moment. When your DNS record is proxied through Cloudflare, that connection ends at our edge. Cloudflare reads the client's HTTP request, applies your security and caching rules, and then makes its own request to your origin over a connection Cloudflare controls. The flow-control frames, pings, settings, and stream resets that the attacker sends are consumed by our edge. They are not forwarded. Your nginx only ever sees the requests Cloudflare chooses to send, framed the way Cloudflare frames them. This also holds when Cloudflare connects to your origin over HTTP/2: Cloudflare runs its own flow control on that connection and sends WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM frames only as its own traffic needs, so a client can't make it relay the billions of WINDOW_UPDATE frames the attack requires. Rapid7 makes the same point in its analysis of CVE-2026-123007: if the HTTP/2 connection is proxied, the attacker's frames "will likely not be retransmitted" in a way that allows exploitation. This breaks each of the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks. CVE What the attacker needs Behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy CVE-2026-123007 Direct control over HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, SETTINGS, PING and RST_STREAM on one connection to nginx Protected. Control frames terminate at Cloudflare's edge. CVE-2026-123633 The first part of a HEADERS frame on a direct HTTP/2 connection, plus the ability to exhaust nginx connection slots and reset the TCP connection Protected. The client's HTTP/2 connection terminates at Cloudflare. CVE-2026-121810 A direct QUIC/HTTP/3 connection to nginx Protected. HTTP/3 terminates at Cloudflare's edge. We do not communicate to origins over HTTP/3 CVE-2026-123634 A request and its mirror or SSI subrequest waiting on the same DNS lookup, and the main request ending while the answer is processed. In Xint's exploit, nginx's resolver had to reach the attacker's DNS server. Not fully protected. Depends on how your config builds proxy_pass. Patch. CVE-2026-113425 A direct IMAP/POP3/SMTP connection to the nginx mail proxy Not protected. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry mail traffic. There is one condition to be protected by Cloudflare here: your origin must not be reachable directly. If an attacker can find your origin's IP and connect to it directly (TCP 443 or 80 for HTTP/2, UDP 443 for HTTP/3, or the mail ports), Cloudflare isn't in the path and the protection doesn't apply. You should ensure that your origin servers can only be accessed through Cloudflare’s proxies, using one of the following approaches: Cloudflare Tunnel. Your origin makes an outbound-only connection to Cloudflare and exposes no inbound ports. Firewall to Cloudflare IP ranges. Accept inbound HTTP/HTTPS only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges. This must be done using an IP firewall, not based on configuration in your nginx server. Authenticated Origin Pulls (mTLS). Your origin rejects any TLS connection that doesn't present Cloudflare's client certificate. Xint's own exposure check makes the same point: "If a CDN or reverse proxy sits in front of nginx, the test only reaches the proxy, so also run it directly against the nginx server." Where the protection does not apply There are several situations in which Cloudflare’s HTTP proxy does not provide protection. Spectrum TCP/UDP applications. For these configurations, traffic from the Internet is passed unmodified through to your origin. If your origin is running nginx, patch or disable the affected features. nginx mail proxy. Cloudflare's HTTP proxy does not carry IMAP, POP3 or SMTP. Restrict mail listeners to trusted networks until patched. CVE-2026-123634 (resolver). This depends on how your configuration builds the proxy_pass target from the request, combined with a carefully timed cancellation of an HTTP request. Passing your traffic through Cloudflare’s proxy makes it harder to exploit this, but does not provide full protection. Update regardless. DNS-only (grey-cloud), internal or non-proxied nginx. Any nginx server an attacker can reach without going through Cloudflare, including internal services behind a compromised host, needs to be patched. Cloudflare’s WAF rules are not relevant to these vulnerabilities. These are protocol-level bugs. Because Cloudflare’s proxy handles parsing the HTTP protocol messages, and creates new messages to fetch information from origin servers, origins behind Cloudflare's HTTP proxy are protected from the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 bugs without needing a rule. We have therefore not released a managed rule. The protection comes from connection termination, not from pattern matching. What to do now Find every nginx server. Include nginx Plus, distribution packages, container images and appliances. Run nginx -V and nginx -T on each and note HTTP/2, HTTP/3/QUIC listeners, proxy_pass with variables plus SSI or mirror, and any mail block. Patch. Update nginx Open Source to 1.30.7 or 1.31.9, nginx Plus to 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1, or your distribution's fixed package. F5 lists nginx Plus R34 to R36 as affected with no fixed build, so move those to a fixed 37.x release. Then restart nginx or complete a binary upgrade. A config reload does not replace the running binary. Check backport versions carefully. Distributions often patch without changing the version nginx -v reports. Compare the full package version against your distribution's advisory. Make sure your origin is only reachable through Cloudflare. Use Tunnel, IP allowlisting or Authenticated Origin Pulls. If you can't patch yet, disable what you don't need. http2 off; (nginx 1.25.1 and later; on older versions, remove http2 from the listen directive) blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Removing QUIC listeners and setting http3 off; blocks CVE-2026-121810. Point proxy_pass at fixed upstream groups for CVE-2026-123634. Don't rely on mirror_request_body alone: Xint's tested setup set it to off, and the default on stopped that exploit, but SSI and other subrequests can still reach the bug. Bind mail listeners to trusted networks for CVE-2026-113425. Restart so old connections close. Block SCTP if you don't use it. Add install sctp /bin/false to a file in /etc/modprobe.d/ to stop the kernel module from loading. This doesn't unload an already-loaded module or disable SCTP built into the kernel. When your distribution ships a kernel update for the SCTP bug, install it and reboot. Blocking the module is a stopgap until then. The Cloudflare Radar Zero Wire entry for nginx2root has the full checklist, a prompt you can give an agent to run a read-only assessment of your fleet, and links to every vendor advisory. Technical deep dive Let’s dig into the details of the five bugs by looking through the code. We’re looking at nginx 1.31.8 (commit 140aa94) which was the most recent code published before the fixes, and comparing this to the fixes in 1.31.9 (which were also included in release 1.30.7 on the stable branch). A note on methodology: we based our analysis on the public advisories, and to verify our reading of the code, we built the public 1.31.8 and 1.31.9 releases with AddressSanitizer and ran tests for four of the five bugs (flow control, HTTP/2 use-after-free, resolver and mail proxy). Each one faults on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. We did not reproduce the HTTP/3 bug; that section is based on the fix commit and the published analysis. One pattern, in four places Four of the five bugs are use-after-free bugs. This is a common issue with programs that manually manage memory without language support: one part of the code frees an object that another part is still using. nginx is event driven. A handler runs, calls other code, and that code returns to the handler. Three of the bugs occur when the called code tears down the connection or request the handler is working on. In the fourth, a second connection still holds a pointer to the object. CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-121810. A request needs a connection slot to reach its upstream. nginx is low on slots, so it closes an idle connection to free one. The connection it chooses is the one the request belongs to. CVE-2026-123634. A resolver callback ends a request. Cleanup of that request frees a second resolver context that the resolver is about to call next. CVE-2026-113425. When a write to a mail client fails, the client connection is closed while the connection to the authentication service still points at its session. F5 rates all four as potential code execution if address space layout randomization (ASLR) is disabled or bypassed, and in its tests Xint reports code execution with the privileges of the nginx worker. The fifth bug, CVE-2026-123007, is of a different kind: an accounting error that becomes a length error. CVE-2026-123007: two flow-control pieces that each look correct HTTP/2 flow control limits the amount of response data a server may send. nginx tracks a send window for each stream and one for the connection, h2c->send_window. The client enlarges a window with a WINDOW_UPDATE frame, and the protocol caps every window at 2^31 − 1. nginx enforces that cap when a WINDOW_UPDATE arrives (ngx_http_v2_state_window_update()): if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) { /* logs "client violated connection flow control" */ return ngx_http_v2_connection_error(h2c, NGX_HTTP_V2_FLOW_CTRL_ERROR); } On its own, this check is correct. But the connection window also grows in a second place. When nginx queues DATA frames for a stream, it subtracts their length from the window. If the stream is canceled before those frames go out, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() takes them off the queue and returns the credit: h2c->send_window += window; Nothing caps this line. As the fix commit describes, if the client enlarges the connection window after the frames are queued and before the stream is terminated, the refund pushes the window past 2^31 − 1. From that point the first check no longer works. h2c->send_window is an unsigned size_t, so NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window wraps around to a very large number and every subsequent WINDOW_UPDATE is accepted. The client can then raise the window as far as it wants. The window is unsigned, but the code that sizes DATA frames compares it as a signed value (ngx_http_v2_send_chain()): if (limit == 0 || limit > (off_t) h2c->send_window) { limit = h2c->send_window; } ... if ((off_t) frame_size > limit) { frame_size = (size_t) limit; } After the window passes 2^63, it is negative as an off_t. The frame size becomes the window value itself, a number between 2^63 and 2^64, and nginx builds a buffer whose last pointer lies before its pos pointer. Over TLS, that buffer reaches a memcpy() in ngx_ssl_send_chain() with that length. Our TLS test stops at that point under AddressSanitizer. Xint's write-up explains how, with the window pushed close to 2^64, this turns into a controlled out-of-bounds write and an address leak, and Xint, Rapid7, and Wiz each report code execution from it. This post goes no further than the fault. Over cleartext HTTP/2, the same invalid buffer follows a different output path. Our cleartext test also faults under AddressSanitizer on 1.31.8 and runs clean on 1.31.9. The public write-ups address the TLS case. How much traffic the known attacks require The biggest step a WINDOW_UPDATE can take is 2^31 − 1, and a WINDOW_UPDATE frame is 13 bytes. Bringing a 64-bit window near its top therefore requires about 2^33 frames: roughly 8.6 billion frames, or about 112 GB (104 GiB). Rapid7, which published a proof of concept, gives the same figure and adds that nginx limits control-frame traffic relative to other traffic on the connection, so its run also sends about 15 GiB of other request traffic. Its total comes to approximately 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: about two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s link and about seventeen minutes at 1 Gbit/s. Rapid7 estimates the WINDOW_UPDATE traffic needed to reach 2^63 at about 2^32 frames, or 52 GiB, half of the 104 GiB figure. It also notes that these figures describe its route and are not a proven minimum. For defenders, this is the useful fact about the bug. At this volume, the known attacks are hard to hide: nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a single client over one long-lived connection and sends little back, much more than the requests in the access log account for. Why it was difficult to find The refund line has existed in nginx since HTTP/2 support arrived in 1.9.5 in 2015. Two things made it difficult to notice. First, each piece looks correct on its own. The check on WINDOW_UPDATE is the right check. The refund is the right refund. The bug is that the check relies on an assumption the refund does not preserve. Second, testing that waits for a crash is very unlikely to reach it, because a crash requires tens of gigabytes of input. The bad state itself can be reached with very little traffic: Censys published a cleartext test that reaches what it calls the corrupted flow-control state with a 5.69 MB capture. A test that asserts "the send window never exceeds its protocol maximum" after every frame would flag the bad state as soon as a test sequence got there. A test that waits for memory corruption would not. The fix The fix (6 lines added) introduces a counter, h2c->send_queued, for DATA that is queued but not yet sent. The WINDOW_UPDATE check now includes those bytes in the window: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window - h2c->send_queued) { From the client's perspective, queued frames still count toward the window, so the client can no longer refill credit that nginx is about to refund. On a fixed version the attempt is rejected with a flow-control error. CVE-2026-123633: where two protections interact An nginx worker has a fixed number of connection slots (worker_connections), which the client and upstream connections share. Since 1.19.2, when free slots run low (1/16 of the total or fewer), ngx_get_connection() calls ngx_drain_connections(), which closes connections marked "reusable": connections with nothing in progress, such as idle keep-alive connections. This works only if a reusable connection truly has nothing in progress. For HTTP/2 that was not always the case. Two commits landed on the same day in February 2021 and were released together in 1.19.7: "HTTP/2: fixed reusing connections with active requests" fixed a case in which a cleartext HTTP/2 connection could remain reusable while it had a request. "HTTP/2: reuse of connections with incomplete frames" registered a connection as reusable while it waits for the remainder of a partly received frame, so that a client cannot hold slots with partial frames. The second change is the relevant one here. As the fix commit explains, if the remainder of that frame is a HEADERS frame, a stream is created, but the reusable status was not reset until the connection next went idle. The connection then has a request and remains in the reusable queue. If that request is proxied, nginx requests a slot for the upstream connection. If slots are short, the drain runs inside that call and can choose this same connection. The drain instructs the connection to close and nginx attempts to send GOAWAY. If that send fails, nginx frees the connection and every stream on it. Control then goes back to the upstream code, which continues to use the request it was called for. Each change made sense on its own. The interaction between them was subtle and stayed unnoticed until this year. F5's advisory credits Albert Ebb of Metnir, Nir Ohfeld at Wiz Research, Xint.io and memN0ps of Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; nginx.org's changelog credits Albert of Vexera AI. The fix Two lines added: ngx_http_v2_create_stream() now calls ngx_reusable_connection(h2c->connection, 0). A connection that has a stream is never reusable, regardless of the state it was in before. CVE-2026-121810: the same idea, in QUIC According to the fix commit and Xint's analysis, the HTTP/3 bug reaches the same result by a different route. In nginx's QUIC code, each QUIC connection uses one connection slot and each stream uses another. A QUIC connection may be drained only when every stream remaining in its tree can be cancelled, and nginx determines this by walking the connection's tree of streams. ngx_quic_create_stream() removes the QUIC connection from the reusable queue and then requests a slot for the new stream. Before the fix, the new stream was added to the tree only after that. If the slot request triggered a drain that closed another, idle stream of the same QUIC connection, the code handling the closed stream walked the tree, did not find the stream being created, concluded the connection was idle, and made it reusable again. A later drain, for example when the new request connects to its upstream, could then close the QUIC connection while that request was running. F5's advisory states that exploitation "also depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control". Xint writes that the bug "is triggered by a slightly different mechanism" from the HTTP/2 one. The fix Four lines added: the stream goes into the tree before the slot is requested, and is taken out again on the error paths. CVE-2026-123634: freeing the next item of a list during the walk When proxy_pass contains a variable, nginx resolves the host name while handling the request. If a lookup for the same name is already in progress, the new request waits on the same resolver node. When the answer arrives, nginx detaches the list of waiting contexts and calls each in turn: next = rn->waiting; rn->waiting = NULL; while (next) { ctx = next; ... next = ctx->next; ctx->handler(ctx); } The loop stores next before the handler call, so a handler may free its own context. The trouble starts when a handler frees a different context in the same list. This happens when two contexts belong to one request, as with a request and its mirror subrequest resolving the same name (the case Xint tested; F5 also lists SSI subrequests). If the first handler ends the request, the request's cleanup calls ngx_resolve_name_done() for the second context. That function searches the node's waiting list for the context, does not find it because the list has been detached, and frees the context regardless. The loop then advances to the freed context. Usually nginx logs this. On vulnerable versions, when the search fails, it writes could not cancel <name> resolving to the error log at alert level. This line is worth searching for. It is not proof either way: the fix commit notes that one variant, while following a CNAME, produced no alert. The fix A context cancelled while it sits in a detached list is no longer freed immediately. Its handler is swapped for one that frees it when the loop gets to it (31 lines added). The fix also downgrades the alert to a debug message, so the line above shows up at alert level only on unpatched versions. CVE-2026-113425: two connections, one session With auth_http, the mail proxy asks an HTTP service to verify each login. During the wait, it holds two connections for one session: the client connection and the connection to the authentication service. The second points at the session and uses the memory pool of the client connection. Before the fix, the reply the protocol handler had prepared for the client remained queued while the authentication request was in progress, and the client's write handler was still ngx_mail_send(). If that handler ran and the write failed because the client had reset the connection, it closed the client connection and destroyed the session. The authentication connection still pointed at the session, and the next event on that connection used freed memory. Xint describes two conditions for this: the client's write event must already be registered (for example, because the client stopped reading replies), and the login command and the reset must be handled in the same pass of the event loop. Valid credentials are not needed, because this happens before the login is checked. The fix Two added lines discard the queued reply when the authentication request begins. The same release contains three further commits that block client writes while the proxy waits for the authentication response, while it connects to the upstream and reads its greeting, and while it resolves an SMTP client's address and name. What the fixes share The five fixes each involve minor corrections to the code. They add between 2 and 31 lines each, and the mail proxy fix came with three further commits. There is no design change needed. Each fix restores an invariant that the rest of the code already depended on: a send window never goes above the protocol maximum a connection with a request in progress is never reusable an object that other code is about to use is not freed out from under it In every case, one code path failed to keep a rule that the rest of the code relied on, and the fix makes that path keep it. As code is modified over time, it is very easy for these kinds of rules to become broken. What to watch for Attempts to exploit this will typically trigger some characteristic log messages. Three of these messages (the two at info and the one at warn) fall below nginx's default error_log level of error and appear only if a lower level is set. The alert messages are logged by default. Bug Log messages or other signals CVE-2026-123007 A single long-lived HTTP/2 connection on which nginx receives tens of gigabytes from a client and sends little back, much more than its logged requests account for. On fixed versions a rejected attempt logs client violated connection flow control: received WINDOW_UPDATE frame with window increment ... not allowed for window ... (level info; older versions have the same message for ordinary violations). http2 flood detected (level info) on such a connection can be a failed attempt, but nginx also logs that message for several other limits. CVE-2026-123633, CVE-2026-121810 worker process <pid> exited on signal 11 (level alert) on servers that accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 and proxy to an upstream, along with worker_connections are not enough, reusing connections (level warn). A use-after-free does not always crash. CVE-2026-123634 could not cancel <name> resolving (level alert, unpatched versions only). The absence of this message does not rule the bug out. CVE-2026-113425 Worker crashes in a mail proxy using auth_http, with client connections reset during login. All five Unexpected programs launched by an nginx worker process, for example from an auditd rule on execve for the worker's user. Xint recommends this check, and it is the strongest sign of a successful attack. Timeline Date (UTC) Event Oct 11, 2026 Xint discovers the vulnerabilities Oct 16, 2026 Reported to F5 via HackerOne Oct 27, 2026 Reports delivered to the nginx development team Nov 10, 2026 Xint completes patch validation Nov 18, 2026 Public disclosure; nginx 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 released The bugs will keep coming CVE-2026-123007 sat in nginx for more than ten years. The SCTP bug has been in the Linux kernel since 2018. Xint says one of its researchers found CVE-2026-123007 by hand and an automated Xint scan found the other four nginx bugs. Several other teams found the two HTTP/2 bugs independently. Meanwhile, nginx's advisory list has gone from two entries in 2025 to 36 so far this year. AI-assisted research is finding bugs in heavily reviewed code faster than before, and more disclosures like this one are coming. That's a large part of why it's worth putting Cloudflare in front of your origin. A protocol bug in your web server becomes much less of a risk when the attacker can't speak that protocol to your server directly. Our edge is not affected, and the HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 attacks against your nginx end at our network. Patch anyway, lock down your origin so Cloudflare is the only way in, and use the Radar Zero Wire page to check your fleet. items.title: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube)
items.content: Token fraud is here and it’s BAD (YouTube) Claire Vo runs ChatPRD, an AI platform that helps product managers "turn an idea into a spec". The product has been live since the GPT-4 era, and Claire has been building it in public for much of that time. In this YouTube video (see also the accompanying Twitter post) Claire describes the flood of token fraud she has seen from groups abusing the product's free trial, sometimes just to get free AI usage but often to resell tokens or run other commercial enterprises on top of the ChatPRD agent. I am funding a international Roblox and Fortnite map studio. They run a loop of free trials and promo codes and then tunnel to my agent and use it to build Roblox and Fortnite maps. Apparently one of the common prompts Claire saw running through her agent involved SVGs of pelicans riding bicycles! Presumably the token scammers are using that to help sniff the underlying models - different model families have a definite signature, and I've used it like this in the past to try and guess the identity of stealth preview models on platforms like OpenRouter. Claire is winding down her free trials entirely, which sadly looks like the right decision in the face of this abuse. Tags: youtube, ai, generative-ai, llms, pelican-riding-a-bicycle, ai-misuse

items.title: LLM Complexity: Towards a Computational Complexity View of Large Language Model Inference
items.author: Yu-Hung Wu, Shao-Xiang Yuan, Chan-Hung Yu, Zih-Ching Chen, Kuan-Hao Huang, Shao-Hua Sun
items.content: Computational complexity theory offers a principled framework for characterizing the efficiency of computational problems, and Large Language Models (LLMs) can similarly be viewed as computational systems executing a structured process of input, inference-time compute, and output. In this context, the number of generated tokens emerges as a natural and directly observable proxy for inference-time compute. However, we show that the tempting analogy between LLM token length and classical time complexity does not hold. We disprove the hypothesis that inference-time token usage aligns monotonically with classical time complexity, demonstrating a fundamental divergence grounded in how LLMs actually allocate computation during inference. To this end, we introduce LLM Complexity, a new metric designed to quantify problem complexity from the perspective of LLMs by characterizing the area bounded above by the accuracy-token curve. We find that diverse LLMs induce highly consistent task rankings under LLM Complexity, indicating that the metric captures stable notions of difficulty across models. We leverage this property to construct an easy-to-hard curriculum for supervised fine-tuning, which improves accuracy while reducing token consumption. Finally, we demonstrate that LLM Complexity generalizes to real-world tasks, producing more stable cross-model correlations than human-annotated difficulty labels.

items.title: ICARE: cross-domain text classification with incremental class-aware representation and distillation learning
items.author: Son Duong, Truong X. Tran, Hai-Anh Tran
items.content: The rise of powerful, fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) necessitates robust natural language inference (NLI) systems. These NLI systems ideally train across various tasks, encompassing diverse concepts like sentiment analysis, news classification, and coreference resolution. However, this continual, multi-tasking approach can lead to catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned tasks are lost, especially in domains lacking specific labels. Rehearsing past examples with labels can further exacerbate this issue by causing overfitting, hindering the system's ability to classify new categories. To tackle these challenges, this research proposes ICARE, a novel framework with two key components: an instance selection module and a knowledge distillation method. The former is based on representation learning, which meticulously selects training examples to present to the NLI system. The latter, knowledge distillation with feature and logit-level transfer, facilitates knowledge transfer between tasks. This leverages pruning techniques and optimized objective functions to transfer both essential feature-level and decision-making (logit-level) knowledge, mitigating catastrophic forgetting while adapting to new patterns. Extensive evaluations on benchmark text classification datasets have demonstrated ICARE's effectiveness. The framework achieves a significant improvement in target accuracy and reduction in the ``forgetting metric''. These results solidify ICARE's ability to preserve and leverage learned knowledge across diverse tasks, ultimately enhancing the adaptability and performance of NLI systems. The source code is available at https://github.com/CongSon01/ICARE_NLP.git

items.title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
items.author: Yu Zou, Yan Chen, Jialei Zeng, Xiaorui Zhou, Aixi Zhong, Qi Zhou, Haoran You, Ke Jiang, Changyu Hu
items.content: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

items.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 4.2, Canon Layers at Scale where Synthetic Pretraining Resonates in Reality
items.author: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu
items.content: Do standard benchmarks see the architectural differences that matter? We study it with 64 from-scratch pretraining runs of Transformers and three linear-model families at 1.3-8B parameters on 1-2T Nemotron-CC tokens, at a cost of roughly 100k USD per 8B run. In academic-scale pretraining (1.3B parameters, 100B tokens), architectural differences can all but disappear when the models are carefully tuned. Instead, at 1-2T tokens they become measurable: Canon layers, which add local token mixing, consistently improve Transformers, saving about 30% of pretraining tokens for the same MMLU accuracy at 8B. We also introduce GLA5 and GDN2, which improve gated linear attention and Gated DeltaNet with low-rank output gates. Surprisingly, with Canon, the simplest linear model, gated linear attention, matches Gated DeltaNet and outperforms Mamba2 even at 8B/1T. Therefore, the extra machinery of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba2 may do little more than mix neighboring tokens. Even at 8B/1T, however, high scores on standard benchmarks can hide weaknesses in basic in-context skills. In particular, linear models that match or beat Transformers on these benchmarks cannot, in fact, reliably retrieve information from a short 500-token context. Moreover, no model, Transformer or linear, reliably beats random guessing on arguably the simplest two-hop question, stated in a few short sentences, even at this scale. These findings $\textbf{challenge traditional architecture research}$ based primarily on standard benchmark scores. In contrast, small synthetic playgrounds, which predicted the architectural differences above at <100M parameters, can reveal what these benchmarks miss. For practitioners, one lesson is to include in-context reasoning examples in pretraining data from an early stage, rather than reserve them for later mid-training, let alone post-training.

items.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
items.author: Seojin Kim, Noseong Park
items.content: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

items.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
items.author: Huy Nghiem, Maria Kostylew, Noam Kolt
items.content: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

items.title: The ROI of Small Examples: Optimizing In-Context Learning Under Token Budgets
items.author: Anxo Perez, Jorge Gab\'in, Javier Parapar
items.content: In-context learning (ICL) improves large language model performance at inference time without updating model parameters. However, these gains are not free: in practical deployments, longer prompts directly increase inference cost and latency. Under a fixed token budget, prompt construction therefore becomes a resource-allocation problem. While prior work has often focused on how many examples to include in ICL, we study the complementary question of whether the available budget is better spent on a few long demonstrations or on a larger number of shorter ones. We study this aspect in question answering (QA), by organizing candidate demonstrations into length-based bins and constructing prompts from examples within the same length range under fixed budgets. Experiments on two QA benchmarks (\textit{Beat the AI} and \textit{Natural Questions}), using six instruction-tuned LLMs, show that shorter demonstrations are generally the most effective use of prompt space. This effect is especially strong on \textit{Beat the AI}, and remains visible on NQ, although gains are smaller and saturate earlier in the long-context setting. An additional natural language inference experiment on ANLI R3 finds that one of the two shorter bins performs best for five of six models, although longer demonstrations remain competitive. Overall, our results highlight demonstration granularity as an important factor in prompt design.

items.title: No-Harm-Jury A Jury-Based Multi-Dimensional Harm Evaluation Framework for Medical AI Responses
items.author: Antonio Puertas Gallardo, Mario Ceresa
items.content: We present No-Harm-Jury, a jury-based automated evaluation framework that scores AI-generated medical responses across seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions using a panel of five diverse language models as independent jurors. Responses generated by Ministral-14B on 3,000 questions drawn from PubMedQA, MedQA, and MedMCQA are scored by five jurors across dimensions of informational, social, psychological, autonomy, economic, privacy, and epistemic harm; the 151 empty responses (98 MedQA, 53 MedM- CQA) are excluded, leaving 2,849 valid samples. The median aggregation robustly suppresses individual juror biases while maintaining coverage through complementary specialisation. No existing system combines all five prop- erties of No-Harm-Jury: automated scalable evaluation, five diverse LLM jurors, robust me- dian aggregation (with a reliability-weighted extension), seven conceptually distinct harm dimensions, and application to medical QA benchmarks.

items.title: CANDID: Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution in Local Computer-Use Agents
items.author: Woongkyu Lee, Jungwook Choi
items.content: We present CANDID (Candidate-Driven Intervention for Disciplined Execution), an execution-control framework designed to enhance the reliability of local computer-use agents (CUAs) in resource-constrained settings. While local CUAs feature robust baseline proficiency in single-step action prediction, they frequently fail at critical junctions due to rigid action loops or premature DONE decisions. Rather than imposing imprecise cognitive loads through textual reflection, CANDID repurposes parallel test-time scaling into a disciplined, execution-level intervention at sparse, failure-prone points. We introduce a loop-recovery mechanism to filter candidates away from repeated behaviors and a conservative, unanimous DONE gating policy that requires absolute consensus to terminate. Experiments on OSWorld demonstrate that CANDID's structural control significantly improves success rates, outperforming feedback-based alternatives with minimal execution overhead.

items.title: Quantifying Cultural-Psychological Constructs in Four Centuries of Ottoman Court Registers
items.author: Sila Mutaf, Enes Y{\i}landilo\u{g}lu, Mohammad Atari
items.content: Populations vary along cultural dimensions such as individualism, collectivism, and honor. But how can these dimensions be studied in historical societies for which conventional psychological data are unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational text-analytic framework for quantifying psychological constructs in 54,670 Ottoman Turkish court records from 21 Istanbul courts spanning 1513-1911 CE. We develop sentence-embedding models adapted to Ottoman legal language and extend a theory-driven, text-analytic pipeline to capture cultural variation along the dimensions of individualism, collectivism, and honor in this historical corpus. We evaluate our models through multiple methods: document retrieval, semantic textual similarity, questionnaire-item classification, and validation against expert annotations. Our adapted sentence transformer (OTA-BERTurk) achieved a Recall@1 of .843 on the test set for document retrieval, a Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) of .806 for semantic textual similarity (meaning the best answer usually appeared as a top result), and classified questionnaire items with 89.58\% accuracy. Document-level performance varied across constructs and methods. Qualitative analysis further showed that high scores reflected historically specific legal and institutional patterns. We publicly release the models, construct representations, scoring pipeline, as well as an interactive web interface to support transparent, reproducible historical-psychological analyses of Ottoman Turkish court records spanning approximately four centuries. These computational tools enable the study of psychological variation across centuries of cultural and institutional change in a diverse empire.

items.title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
items.author: Frederik Hauke, Jan Clusmann, Hanna Kreutzer, Christiane Kuhl, Tianyu Han, Felix Barajas Ordonez, Sven Nebelung, Jakob Nikolas Kather, Daniel Truhn
items.content: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

items.title: PsyWorld: Profile-Conditioned World Modeling for Human Behavior Prediction
items.author: Ziyuan Qin, Yang Qiao, Summer B. Frandsen, Michael T. Treadway, Liang Zhao
items.content: Understanding how stable psychometric traits and time-varying states jointly inform behavior is an important problem in computational behavioral science. Existing personalized agents commonly condition actions directly on a static profile, leaving realized state transitions unused as an explicit source of supervision. We introduce a profile-conditioned state world model that uses observed environment--behavior state transitions to learn transition-informed representations for behavioral prediction. During training, a posterior encoder quantizes realized transitions, while a prior predicts the resulting codes from the psychometric profile and pre-transition context. The prior code and predicted next state then condition macro-level behavior and simulator-grounded execution. Thus, the world model provides structured transition supervision instead of treating personality as a direct action descriptor. We evaluate the framework in VEET, a controlled behavioral simulator with human trajectories, and in AgentSociety as a structurally different synthetic environment. A participant-disjoint split of 240 training, 25 validation, and 48 test participants evaluates generalization to unseen people. On VEET, the model reaches 0.904 Top-1 accuracy (95\% CI: [0.895, 0.913]) and 0.0033 Macro KL. Ablations associate continuous next-state modeling with most of the Top-1 gain, while discrete codes and prior alignment mainly improve Top-3 and distributional alignment. These results establish transition-informed world-model supervision as useful for subject-generalized behavior prediction, without implying causal psychological mechanisms or calibrated long-horizon state dynamics.

items.title: Watch Where You Linearize: Predicting and Correcting Model-Merging Interference
items.author: Ido Nitzan Hidekel, Dan Raviv
items.content: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models by adding their task vectors to a shared backbone. Interference is typically assessed only after constructing and evaluating a candidate merge, making coefficient search expensive. We show that a first-order directional derivative of task A's outputs along task B's vector can predict interference, but only when evaluated at the appropriate model. At the receiver model, this derivative forecasts nearby merges per task and per example, halves the accuracy error of a no-change baseline, and identifies most examples whose predictions flip. For full multi-task merges, a single evaluation is insufficient; two evaluations along the merge path are needed. At the shared pretrained backbone, however, the derivative is nearly orthogonal to realized changes in our vision experiments and only partly predictive in LoRA language-model pilots. Controls link this failure to displacement along the receiver's own task vector, not simply parameter distance; the mismatch appears within the first few dozen fine-tuning steps. Freezing receiver-local responses produces a surrogate affine in the merge coefficients. We use it to construct LR-Merge, a label-free correction that optimizes coefficients through convex teacher matching on unlabeled probes, without backpropagation through merged networks. LR-Merge improves all tested closed-form, isotropic, and sparsified base mergers, with gains generally increasing as more tasks are merged. Using pretrained rather than receiver-local responses instead degrades the base merge. LR-Merge matches exact teacher matching through a merged network, which takes roughly three times longer to converge and performs similarly at an equal compute budget. Once built, the surrogate answers new coefficient and task-subset queries in seconds.

items.title: Density Feedback Control for Transferability of Generative Sparse Adversarial Attacks
items.author: Dongsu Song, Jay Hoon Jung
items.content: Generator-based sparse adversarial attacks train encoder--decoder networks to produce transferable sparse perturbations for black-box robustness evaluation. Their perturbation density, however, is set only indirectly by a fixed sparsity coefficient whose mapping to density is unknown and shifts during training, so reaching a target density requires re-tuning; this fixed pressure also yields little transferability gain once density reduction begins. We propose Density Feedback Control (DFC), which tightens or relaxes this coefficient at the end of each epoch according to the gap between the observed hard-mask density and the target, without changing the generator architecture or loss. At a 10\% target density, DFC brings the mean density of three base attacks within one percentage point of the target in a single run and improves the transfer attack success rate (ASR) of two of them on CNN and Transformer targets, including under per-image $\ell_0$ budgets, while perturbing fewer pixels. Tracing GPG's training, we observe that as DFC relaxes the coefficient, the transfer ASR recovers with the density and overtakes the fixed-coefficient baseline with fewer pixels. For EGS-TSSA, which restricts perturbations to source-model feature-importance regions, DFC yields no consistent gain; we analyze how this restriction interacts with density feedback.

items.title: A Model of Diverse Sampling from Language Models
items.author: Manuel Prada-Corral, Yahya Emara, Timothy J. O'Donnell, Ryan Cotterell, Tim Vieira
items.content: Language models often produce high-quality individual samples but poor sets, with repeated samples clustering around the same semantic modes. We formalize diverse generation as sampling a size-$K$ subset of complete strings from a determinantal point process (DPP), where the likelihood encodes item quality, and the embedding geometry encodes repulsion between similar outputs. Exact inference over all strings is intractable, so we propose PoolDPP: draw a finite candidate pool from a tractable proposal, importance-weight the candidates toward the target quality, and run a $K$-DPP sampler on the induced pool kernel; a greedy MAP variant provides deterministic selection. We prove a finite-sample bound with an explicit constant: the KL divergence between the sampler's output and the target $K$-DPP decays as O(1/N) in the pool size. Empirically, PoolDPP extends the quality--diversity frontier on open-ended generation and the precision--recall frontier on ambiguous text-to-SQL (Ambrosia), and on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K), it raises diversity at about the same pass@$K$.

items.title: On the Impact of Feature Reduction Techniques on Adversarial Attacks
items.author: Mohammad Meymani, Roozbeh Razavi-Far
items.content: Adversarial attacks have posed significant threats to machine learning models by exploiting their inherent vulnerabilities. Researchers have established an interdisciplinary field called adversarial machine learning to explore these vulnerabilities and develop corresponding defense strategies. Feature reduction strategies are used to decrease the dimensionality of the data in order to reduce training time, avoid the curse of dimensionality, prevent overfitting, and mitigate redundant features. However, their effect on adversarial robustness across different classifiers and attack scenarios remains insufficiently explored. This study aims to analyze the effect of feature reduction techniques on the adversarial robustness of a diverse set of machine learning models under poisoning, backdoor, and universal adversarial perturbation attacks on the APT dataset. These models include support vector machine, decision tree, random forest, multi-layer perceptron, and k-nearest neighbors. The attained results are compared with scenarios where different feature reduction techniques are applied, including principal component analysis, permutation importance ranking, recursive feature elimination, and univariate mutual information. Metrics such as accuracy, F1-score, and mitigation score are employed to evaluate the effect of these techniques on adversarial robustness. The results demonstrate that permutation importance ranking and univariate mutual information generally provide the most consistent robustness improvements, while other methods exhibit more variable effects depending on the classifier and attack scenario.

items.title: Near-Quadratic Sample Compression for All VC Classes
items.author: Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta, Shay Moran, Grigoris Velegkas, Di Wang, Manfred K. Warmuth
items.content: The sample compression conjecture is a longstanding open problem in learning theory, originating in the work of Littlestone and Warmuth in the 1980s. At its heart is a connection between simplification and generalization: if a predictor consistent with a training sample is defined using only a small part of that sample, then it is likely to generalize. Sample compression schemes formalize this idea, and many natural learning algorithms can be analyzed this way. The sample compression conjecture of Floyd and Warmuth (1995) asserts that every binary concept class of VC dimension $d$ admits a sample compression scheme of size $O(d)$; a weaker conjecture asks only for size polynomial in $d$. Both have remained open: the first bound depending only on $d$, due to Moran and Yehudayoff (2016), is exponential in $d$. We prove the weaker conjecture by constructing a sample compression scheme of size $O(d^2 \log^2 d)$.

items.title: Closing the Analyze-to-Design Gap: An Authorization-Bounded Agent for Self-Driving Laboratories
items.author: Yimeng Liu, Eric Isbrandt, Felix Katzenburg, Kevin P. Greenman, Han Hao, Yang Cao, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik
items.content: Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly integrated into self-driving laboratories (SDLs) to plan experiments and interpret results. However, analytical reasoning alone does not make a laboratory autonomous: autonomy in an SDL is achievable only when the agent can be trusted to act on physical hardware unsupervised and knows when to defer to a human. Here, we present an architecture that integrates an agent at the Analyze-Design interface of the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, enabling agent-driven measurement selection and data interpretation while ensuring that state-changing operations are authorized, validated, and auditable. We demonstrate this architecture on a liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) instrument in an oxidant-screening campaign for synthesizing an organic dye. Within human-defined campaign limits, the agent submitted measurement jobs, interpreted mass spectrometry (MS) and diode-array detection (DAD) data, flagged failed experiments, and produced an oxidant ranking. This ranking matched that obtained from scripted peak integration, and organic chemists confirmed the agent's spectral interpretations and failure assignments. In a simulated environment that replays the archived LC-MS data, where the agent chose which wells to inject under varying injection limits, it measured the highest-yielding condition at about its seventh injection, against 14.5 on average for a random order, and identified it in every campaign with a limit of eight or more injections. An agent can therefore close the analysis-to-design gap while its actions stay bounded and verifiable, which is a step toward greater autonomy for SDLs.

items.title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
items.author: Nianjun Zhou, Dhaval Patel
items.content: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

items.title: FinVeriQA: Financial Research Agents for Question Answering: Routing, Retrieval, MCP Tool Use, and Provenance-Aware Evidence Verification
items.author: Meenakshi Rajpurohit, Anna Phan, Ravikumar Komandur Narayanan, Gunanidhi Ramakrishnan, Nathan Howland
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) write fluent financial analyses but miscompute ratios, recall stale prices, and route questions to the wrong tool with high confidence. We ask which component should do each job in a financial question-answering assistant, and study it with FinVeriQA, an open-source multi-agent research prototype over SEC filings and live market data: a compact typed-decision model (Laya) routes each question and screens out advice requests, Python computes every number, retrieval and tools fetch evidence, Mistral-7B writes a cited answer, a code validator checks that cited IDs exist and that numbers match computed notes, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server exposes the pipeline. In live experiments, Laya routed better than Mistral-7B (0.85 vs. 0.52; overall 0.86 vs. 0.68, McNemar p = 0.0003); a 12B Mistral decided no better, and DeepSeek-R1-8B decided better (0.79 vs. 0.68, p = 0.0192) but about 9.9 times more slowly. Mistral-7B computed 29% of 100 financial calculations correctly against 100% for Python, a live quote cut price error from 210% to 0.00%, and hybrid retrieval reached 76% Hit@5 on 50 filing questions. Yet in a live case study, both agent answers passed validation while describing AMD sample data under NVIDIA's and Alphabet's names. A controlled upper-bound study on the FinRank benchmark explains why: when one figure in the shared evidence is corrupted, self-consistency stays confident (agreement 0.55 to 0.59 while accuracy falls from 0.50 to 0.00), and a shared-evidence check (the kind our validator performs) catches 35% of the errors, whereas a check against the original passage catches 77% ($p = 5.96 \times 10^{-8}$); for DeepSeek-R1-8B, 68% vs. 90%. Verification must be independent of the evidence the writer saw.

items.title: SailSearch: Agent-Assisted Discovery in Combinatorial Optimization
items.author: Dhriti Verma, Kanthi Sarpatwar, Vinicius Lima, Dzung Phan, Jayant Kalagnanam
items.content: We present SailSearch, a human-guided workflow for algorithmic research with two language-model agents, and report results on Market Split and maximum independent set (MIS). For Market Split, our randomized algorithm searches across multiple lattice bases, dividing computation between enumeration and continued basis reduction. Across ten random seeds per instance, it found the first reported CPU-only solutions to 18 of 33 previously open QOBLIB instances, solving 130 to 133 of the 156 benchmark instances per seed with a 24-hour cutoff on two CPU cores. For MIS, our generator encodes planted XOR constraints as graphs with certified optima; on seven instances with 1,752 to 3,996 vertices, the best solutions returned by the tested solvers in eight-hour runs were 5 to 15 vertices below the optimum.

items.title: BuggyMLE: Scaling Machine Learning Engineering Difficulty with Bug Injection
